human_tolerance.notes: Strongly synanthropic: it has benefited from human changes to the environment and many live in highly modified habitats such as city suburbs, farms and pastures, and it is the national bird of Argentina. Nests are built on trees, fence posts, telephone poles and buildings, so it settles readily in developed areas.

phases.name: territorial
phases.note: Monogamous pairs hold territory and sing all year; this is the non-breeding half of the cycle.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Breeds in the austral summer, laying eggs between August and December; a clutch is two to four eggs laid every second day, incubated for 14-18 days.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Chicks are fed for 23-26 days before fledging; young then stay in the natal territory for around six months, sometimes until the following breeding season.

vocalizations.description: The far-carrying ringing roll-call that is the best-known sound of the Argentine countryside, sung year-round as a duet by both sexes from a perch or an exposed branch. The sexes are distinguishable: the male's trill is faster than the female's, and both beat their wings at their sides at the rate of their own trill.

A loud, emphatic call given by a perched bird that has noticed a threat, which also alerts nearby horneros; the referenced recording is of a bird calling from a low shrub at a raptor passing overhead.

taxonomy.note: GBIF backbone gives Passeriformes / Furnariidae / Furnarius, authorship '(Gmelin, 1788)' and taxonomicStatus ACCEPTED; ITIS gives '(J. F. Gmelin, 1788)'. No synonym handling is needed.

external.note: GBIF usage key 2485821 and iNaturalist taxon id 11275 from the issue's data pointers, both confirmed against the GBIF backbone record. ITIS TSN 560127 (Wikidata P815, confirmed against the ITIS search service). Wikidata Q852731, NCBI Taxonomy 81886 (P685) and eBird code rufhor2 (P3444) from Wikidata.

common_names.note: Portuguese, French, German and Dutch names from the Wikidata labels for Q852731; the Spanish name 'hornero común' from the Spanish Wikipedia article, which opens 'El hornero común'. The English name follows the issue title and the English Wikipedia article, with capitalisation normalised to sentence case.

conservation.note: Wikipedia: 'It is not threatened by human activities and is listed as least concern by the IUCN.' The IUCN assessment id (22702144) is carried in Wikidata (P627) and matches the citation in the article; the Red List page itself is not used as a source because it is not openly licensed.

range.note: Country list derived from 'Its range includes midwestern, southeastern, and southern Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, Uruguay, and northern and central Argentina, extending as far south as northern Patagonia.'

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Walk is sourced: the species obtains its food 'by foraging on the ground while walking'. Hop is authored rather than sourced; it is kept because the shared perching-songbird program feeds on the ground with the hop gait, and a small passerine that walks over open ground also hops.

traits.nest_type.note: The nest is 'a large thick clay "oven" placed on a tree, or man-made structures such as fence posts, telephone poles, or buildings'. A mud oven is a self-built mass on a support rather than a woven cup or an existing cavity, so Platform is the closest of the schema's types.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg: 46.42 g sits below the 0.05 kg boundary the validator uses for Tiny.

traits.mass_kg.note: EltonTraits BirdFuncDat species-level BodyMass-Value 46.42 g (BodyMass-Source Dunning 2008, CRC Handbook of Avian Body Masses, which Wikipedia also cites). Wikipedia independently gives 31-58 g with males heavier, so 46.42 g sits inside that range.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: 31 to 58 g, citing Ridgely & Tudor (1994, 2009) and Dunning (2008).

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of '18 to 20 centimetres', citing Ridgely & Tudor (1994, 2009) and Dunning (2008).

traits.wingspan_m.note: Judgement, and a scale estimate rather than a measurement. No open-licensed source gives a wingspan for F. rufus: English and Spanish Wikipedia, Wikidata and the GBIF backbone carry none, and the only figures found were in field guides and a longevity/measurements database that are not openly licensed. The value is derived from length_m by the span-to-length ratio of a comparable open-source record of the same build and family order, the European blackbird (0.36 m span over 0.2625 m length = 1.371), applied to 0.19 m and rounded to 0.26 m. For reference the same ratio across the repo's other open-source passerines runs from 1.27 (magpie) to 1.74 (great tit, short round wings), so 1.37 is mid-range. Correct this if a measured value turns up.

traits.lifespan_y.note: Judgement. No open-licensed source gives a longevity figure for F. rufus: neither the English nor the Spanish Wikipedia article, Wikidata nor the GBIF backbone carries one, and the field-guide and longevity-database pages that do were not openly licensed. 3.0 years is a typical mean wild passerine value, chosen because the species is a long-lived, sedentary, territory-holding pair bird. Treat it as an order-of-magnitude placeholder, not a measurement.

traits.diet.note: EltonTraits Diet-Inv 80, Diet-Seed 20, Diet-5Cat Invertebrate, Diet-Certainty A. Wikipedia agrees: the species feeds 'on insects and other arthropods obtained by foraging on the ground while walking', and takes 'scraps such as bread crumbs'. The 0.8/0.2 split is therefore the dataset's, not an estimate.

traits.social.note: 'The species is monogamous and the pair bond is long-term, sometimes for life' and 'Pairs remain together throughout the year'. group_size extends past the pair because 'young may stay in their natal territory until the following breeding season', giving a pair with one or two young.

traits.activity_pattern.note: EltonTraits Nocturnal 0. Wikipedia describes all singing, feeding and nest-building as daytime activity and places the loud duet in daylight hours.

traits.defense.note: Authored: the species is a shy, fast, ground-flushing bird that leaves cover when a threat approaches, rather than freezing, mobbing or using a chemical defence.

traits.wariness.note: Very low, from the article's account of a synanthropic bird: it 'has benefited from human changes to the environment and many live in highly modified habitats, such as city suburbs', and it nests on buildings, fence posts and telephone poles. Judgement: 0.1, at the tame end of the scale.

habitat.use.note: ForStrat-ground 70, ForStrat-understory 30, both at species level (ForStrat-SpecLevel 1). Understory is mapped to the arboreal stratum, as in the other bird records.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Authored, from the habitat description 'savannas, second-growth scrub, pastures, and agricultural land'; the bird roosts low in scrub and trees and uses its own nest year-round.

habitat.resources.note: Food weights follow the EltonTraits diet split (invertebrate 0.8, seed 0.2) with no seasonal restriction, since the bird is resident year-round. The nest_platform resource is the mud oven, which Wikipedia says is built on trees, fence posts, telephone poles or buildings; the perch and shrub_thicket shelter weights are authored from the same habitat description.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: urban_affinity Exploiter from the article's explicit statements that the species is 'synanthropic', 'has benefited from human changes to the environment', lives in 'highly modified habitats, such as city suburbs', and is the national bird of Argentina. uses_gardens follows from the same account plus the bird's use of 'pastures, and agricultural land'.

seasonal.strategy.note: ActiveYearRound: the article describes no migration, and says 'Pairs remain together throughout the year and will work on the nest during that time'.

seasonal.phases.note: Breeding window and clutch dates are from 'laying eggs between August and December', 'a clutch generally contains two to four eggs', 'incubated for 14-18 days' and 'Chicks are fed for 23-26 days before fledging'. The young window wraps the year end because 'young birds remain in the parental territory for around 6 months after fledging and sometimes until the following breeding season'. The territorial phase covers the remainder and is the default for a resident pair.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Egg duration is the midpoint of the 14-18 day incubation; the juvenile duration of 180 days is the 'around 6 months' the young remain in the natal territory, and the 0.9 scale reflects the smaller, paler juvenile described in the article.

vocalizations.song.note: The Commons recording is captioned 'Song and call of Furnarius rufus' and documents the call; the description of the sexually distinct duet, the wingbeat at the rate of the trill, and the year-round loudness are from the article's account of the species' songs.

vocalizations.alarm.note: The xeno-canto recording is captioned as an adult alerting its group while Harris's hawks flew past, which documents the alerting call; the description is limited to that behaviour and to the article's account of a loud, emphatic call.

look.note: Plumage from the article: 'rufous-brown back and pale buffy brown underparts', a 'dull brown crown', a 'whitish throat', 'blackish' flight feathers with 'cinnamon wingbars', a horn-coloured bill 2.5 cm long, and a short square tail 7.1 cm long on an 18-20 cm bird. Proportions are authored: long body and long legs for a ground-walking ovenbird, small head, short tail, and a long slender slightly decurved bill. Only one extra part is used (a pale throat) to keep the mesh free of parts that clip each other.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared perching-songbird program. flee_m and food_tag are authored; food_tag follows the 0.8 invertebrate share of the diet. nest_m1/nest_m2 (8-11) follow the August-December laying window, which the program uses to gate nest building. song_cooldown_s is set below the program default of 8 s because the hornero is among the most persistently vocal birds in its range and sings its duet year-round. No bespoke behavior.json is needed.
